newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-EMI shareholders set for 500 mln pound bonus.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EMI shareholders set for 500 mln pound bonus.

text.p: British music company EMI Group Plc is planning to return around 500 million pounds ($820 million) to shareholders, the company said on Tuesday.
EMI, one of the six major companies dominating the global music industry, also announced a restructuring of its North American music operations, slicing out a layer of management.
EMI took a provision of 117.2 million pounds in its last financial year to cover the cost of office closures and asset write-offs relating to the restructuring.

Pre-tax profit excluding exceptional items rose 3.6 percent to 380.5 million pounds in the year to end-March. Pre-tax profit totalled 283.9 million once exceptional items were included and the company increased its dividend 11 percent to 30 pence per share. EMI, which has the Beatles catalogue and modern-day artists such as The Spice Girls on its roster, made a downbeat forecast for the current year.
"Given the strength of sterling and subdued industry conditions, progress in the current year is likely to be modest," the company said.
EMI shares, which have underperformed the media sector by 13 percent since the company was demerged from Thorn EMI last August, fell 24.5p to 1196.5p by 1025 GMT.
The charge and worries over the impact of sterling depressed the price but analysts said the plan to return capital limited the downside.
Chairman Sir Colin Southgate told Reuters that the currency factor was likely to wipe some 30 million pounds off profits this year, similar to its impact last year.
The global music market is worth some $40 billion annually but its rate of growth has dropped back well into single figures after several years of increases in excess of 10 percent.
Southgate said he expected growth ultimately to return to seven-eight percent but "not this year".
EMI hopes to have its proposals to return capital to shareholders ready in time for its July 18 annual meeting and implement them shortly afterwards.

It plans to return up to 10 percent of its market value -- a total of around 500 million pounds. Southgate said this was a "substantial" sum but added that EMI had assessed what it needed for its music businesses and HMV retail arm before deciding on the move.
The North American restructuring is designed to cut costs, improve links with other parts of the group and begin a process of management renewal.

Ken Berry, who heads EMI Music International and Virgin Records, has been appointed worldwide president of EMI Recorded Music, adding control of the EMI Capitol label to his existing responsibilities. He will continue to report to Jim Fifield, CEO of EMI Music.
EMI expects the changes to cut operating costs by 35-40 million pounds annually, just under half of that amount coming this year.
Southgate said he intends to retire in July 2000, and added that the U.S. shake-up was part of a three-year plan.

EMI is the only music major not part of a larger group and as such has long been seen as a takeover target. The decline in its share price in recent months is partly due to the failure of a bidder to emerge.
Southgate flatly denied rumours that EMI had held merger talks with Canadian drinks and entertainment group Seagram .($ = 0.610 British Pounds)
